title: Negation and Possessives
summary: Make sentences negative with não and show possession with meu, seu, nosso, and related forms.

sections.heading: Basic negation with não
sections.body: Put **não** before the verb to make a sentence negative. In conversation, Brazilians often reinforce it with a second **não** at the end.

sections.heading: Possessive adjectives
sections.body:
Possessives agree with the thing possessed, not with the owner. **Seu/sua/seus/suas** can mean your, his, her, or their, so context matters.

| Owner | Masculine | Feminine |
|---|---|---|
| eu | meu(s) | minha(s) |
| você/ele/ela | seu(s) | sua(s) |
| nós | nosso(s) | nossa(s) |

examples.en: My key is in the purse.

sections.heading: Avoiding ambiguity with dele/dela
sections.body: Because **seu/sua** can be ambiguous, Brazilians often use **dele**, **dela**, **deles**, or **delas** after the noun to mean his/her/their.

examples.pt: A mãe dela mora em Recife.

keyPoints: Spoken Brazilian Portuguese may repeat não at the end for emphasis.
Possessives agree with the possessed noun: meu livro, minha casa.
Use dele/dela when seu/sua would be ambiguous.
